questions.q: Why does this lesson say build vs. buy is a comparison of two cost curves rather than two price tags?
options: Because Salesforce prohibits comparing AppExchange pricing to custom development cost directly
Because custom builds never have any ongoing cost once initially developed
Because AppExchange packages are always more expensive than custom builds over any time horizon

Because buying usually means lower upfront cost with a recurring, headcount-scaling subscription, while building means higher upfront cost but potentially a flatter long-run cost without a forever subscription
questions.explain: A subscription's cost compounds over years and with user growth, while a custom build's bigger upfront investment can pay off with a flatter long-run curve -- which is why a five-year total cost comparison tells a very different story than comparing sticker prices alone.

questions.q: What does 'the functional-fit test' mean, as described in this lesson?
options: Scoring how much of a documented requirements list an available package actually covers out of the box or through supported configuration, versus how much needs workarounds or is simply missing
Checking whether a package passed Salesforce's AppExchange security review
Measuring how fast a managed package installs compared to a custom build
Testing whether a package's Apex source code compiles without errors
questions.explain: The functional-fit test is a concrete coverage check against the org's own requirements list -- high honest coverage favors buying and configuring around the gap; low coverage favors custom development.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is a real constraint of choosing a managed package, beyond its subscription price?
options: Managed packages cannot be installed in a production org, only in sandboxes
Managed packages typically hide their Apex source and are customized only through whatever configuration points or APIs the vendor exposes, constraining you to their data model and release cadence
Managed packages are never allowed to store any customer data
Managed packages automatically expire after one year regardless of subscription status
questions.explain: A managed package is namespaced and vendor-owned -- subscribers generally can't see or edit its Apex, so customization is limited to the vendor's exposed extension points, and the org is constrained to the vendor's roadmap and data model.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is custom development usually the stronger candidate over buying a package?
options: Whenever the requirement is common and shared across many organizations
Whenever the AppExchange package's security review has already been completed
When the requirement is unusual, deeply tied to a proprietary process, or central to the organization's actual competitive differentiation
Only when the organization has no in-house developers at all
questions.explain: Commodity functionality is a strong buy candidate since there's little competitive advantage in rebuilding it. A proprietary, differentiating process is a stronger build candidate because a generic package was unlikely to fit it well in the first place.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say build vs. buy is not a one-time, permanent decision?
options: Because Salesforce requires all build-vs-buy decisions to be re-approved annually by policy
Because custom-built features cannot be modified once deployed to production
Because AppExchange packages are automatically uninstalled after three years
Because an org that buys a package as a good fit today may outgrow that fit as its needs diverge from the vendor's roadmap, at which point rebuilding can become the right call
questions.explain: The conditions that made 'buy' correct the first time -- functional fit, cost curve, exit cost -- can change as the org's needs evolve, which is why the lesson recommends tracking what made the original decision correct so you can tell when it's time to revisit it.
